title: Be careful with Visual Studio Code extensions…
summary: Visual Studio Code extensions run with full IDE privileges and pose security risks if compromised, as demonstrated by a malware-infected Nx Console extension that compromised GitHub. The post explains multiple strategies to control extension deployment, including allowlist policies, file system permissions, WDAC, private marketplaces, and Azure Artifacts.
key_points: VS Code extensions are not sandboxed and have full access to the file system, terminal, and credential stores, making them security-critical targets.
Version 1.96+ introduces extensions.allowed policy enforceable via Group Policy to whitelist approved extensions and control auto-updates.
File system permissions via icacls and Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) can block unauthorized .vsix file installations.
Private VS Code marketplace (for GitHub Enterprise) and Azure Artifacts provide controlled, private distribution channels for extensions.
Developer machines accumulate secrets and control the supply chain start, making them equally critical to production infrastructure security.

quotes.text: A compromised extension is just a Node.js process running inside a trusted application, with the same access rights as the developer.
quotes.why_it_matters: Clarifies the attack mechanism: malware executes with full developer privileges, exploiting VS Code's trust model.
